concept.name: Correlation
concept.definition: A statistical measure of the strength and direction of association between two variables, expressed as a dimensionless coefficient bounded in [-1, +1]. The most common form is the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, which measures linear association; rank-based variants (Spearman, Kendall) measure monotonic association.
concept.intuition: It tells you whether two series tend to move together (+1), in opposite directions (-1), or without any linear pattern (0). In markets it describes how strongly two assets' returns co-move, which is the statistical basis of diversification.
concept.mechanics: For the Pearson form, the covariance of the two variables is normalized by the product of their standard deviations, producing a unit-free coefficient in [-1, 1]. Rank correlations convert the observations to ranks before applying the same computation.
concept.formula: rho(X,Y) = Cov(X,Y) / (sigma_X * sigma_Y); sample estimate r = SUM[(x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar)] / sqrt( SUM(x_i - x_bar)^2 * SUM(y_i - y_bar)^2 ), where x_bar and y_bar are the sample means.
concept.failure_modes: The Pearson coefficient only captures linear dependence, so r near 0 can coexist with a strong nonlinear relationship, and a single extreme observation can dominate the estimate. Financial return correlations are also unstable over time and tend to jump toward 1 during crises, exactly when diversification is most needed.
concept.misconceptions: Correlation does not imply causation: a high correlation between two assets or between an indicator and returns does not mean one drives the other. Nor does a high historical correlation guarantee that the relationship will persist out of sample.
concept.example: The daily returns of two large bank stocks over one year have r = 0.82, indicating strong co-movement; combining them in a portfolio delivers far less diversification than pairing a bank with a utility stock at r = 0.15.
